title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
content:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.
Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September, which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.
Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.
As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.
Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.
The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

report.summary: Google launched computer use in Gemini's macOS app, letting its AI perform multistep tasks across native apps, files, and websites in the background.
report.background: Google's move comes as leading AI labs race to turn chatbots into agents that can actually execute work, not just answer questions. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already shipped agentic desktop features, making Google a late entrant in this specific category. Google has been building toward this with Gemini 'Tasks,' which helps users sign into sites, make purchases, and book appointments, and with its 'CC' family organizer agent announced in September. Computer use is a more ambitious step: it lets an AI operate a user's Mac directly, bridging local files, native applications, and the web. The launch also reflects a broader industry shift toward subscription-backed agent products that promise to automate repetitive knowledge work.
key_points: Gemini's computer-use feature runs tasks in the background while showing a live preview in the chat. Users can keep using their screen and cursor for other work, and they can pause, stop, or approve Gemini's actions before they happen, giving them a layer of control over the agent.

The feature is initially limited to English in the U.S. It requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. Google did not provide a timeline for expanding computer use to other markets or platforms, so most users cannot access it yet.

Google positions the feature for tedious, repetitive workflows: filling out forms, applying the same task across batches of files, organizing files into folders by criteria, and creating slideshows from local files or online dashboards. These are practical automation use cases rather than fully open-ended autonomy.

Google is late relative to OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, which already offer agentic desktop features. The launch fits Google's broader agent push, including Gemini Tasks and the early-test 'CC' agent, as it tries to turn Gemini into an execution layer across apps and services.

The design emphasizes user oversight: the agent works in a live preview, and users can intervene before actions occur. That control model is important because computer-use agents can interact with sensitive files, websites, and accounts, raising privacy and security concerns that Google will need to address as usage expands.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals that competition is moving from model quality and chat interfaces to execution: who can reliably operate a computer, integrate with apps, and earn user trust. Google's distribution and subscription base could make it a strong challenger despite being late. For developers, desktop agents create pressure to design apps, permissions, and APIs that are automation-friendly, auditable, and safe, while opening opportunities in workflow automation and agent orchestration. For regular users, the promise is less repetitive work, but the trade-off is granting an AI access to files, accounts, and browsers. The U.S.-only, Mac-only, paid-tier launch means adoption will start narrow, and trust will depend on clear controls, transparency, and strong security defaults.
report.tools: Watch Gemini's Mac app and its Tasks feature as Google expands agentic access. Compare with OpenAI's computer-use/Operator offerings, Anthropic's Claude computer use, and Meta's agent features. For hands-on exploration, open-source projects such as Browser Use, Open Interpreter, UI-TARS, and Skyvern show how agents control browsers and desktops; test them in sandboxed environments and review permission and logging models before relying on them.
